messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 70

# Clinical Vignette: Matiu

Matiu is a 45-year-old Māori man who works as a head chef at a well-regarded restaurant in the city. He carries himself with the quiet authority of someone who has spent decades commanding a kitchen — precise, controlled, rarely rattled. That composure, he admits, is something he has worked hard to maintain. Underneath it, things have been falling apart for years.

When Matiu was 38, he was sexually assaulted by a man he considered a close friend and colleague — someone he had worked alongside for nearly a decade. It happened after a late shift, after drinks, in circumstances Matiu still struggles to piece together in any order that makes sense to him. He has never used the word *rape* in session without first going silent for a long moment. He says the word feels like it belongs to someone else's story. He spent the better part of two years telling himself it didn't count, that he should have been able to stop it, that men don't talk about things like this. He told no one.

In the months that followed, he threw himself into work. The kitchen became the one place where the noise in his head had somewhere to go. He controlled temperatures, timing, the movements of his staff. He was brilliant at it. He was also drinking heavily most nights, sleeping three or four hours if he was lucky, and quietly withdrawing from everyone who cared about him. His marriage, already strained by the long hours of hospitality, did not survive. His ex-wife has said she never really understood what happened to him. He doesn't blame her. He wasn't able to explain it.

Now, seven years on, Matiu describes a life that functions on the surface and fractures underneath. He still runs his kitchen with precision, but certain things undo him without warning. The smell of a particular brand of whiskey sends his body into a state he can only describe as *shutting down* — his hands go cold, his chest tightens, and he has to leave the floor. A new kitchen hand who laughed in a particular way — loud, sudden, familiar — had Matiu gripping the edge of a prep bench and breathing through what he now recognises as a panic response. He said nothing to the young man. He never does.

At night, he does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart pounding, the sheets damp, fragments of memory pressing in that he cannot fully see but cannot escape. He lies in the dark of his apartment and waits for morning. He has stopped trying to fight it. He keeps the television on low so there is something other than his own thoughts in the room.

Matiu describes a persistent sense of shame that he finds almost impossible to articulate — not just about what happened, but about the fact that it still has this much power over him. He is a grown man. He runs a kitchen of fifteen people. He has cooked for dignitaries. And yet he cannot sit with his back to a door, cannot let anyone stand too close behind him in a confined space, cannot watch certain scenes in films without leaving the room. He finds himself irritable in ways that frighten him — short with his staff, sometimes cold in ways he regrets afterward. He describes feeling cut off from things that used to matter: his connection to his whānau has thinned, he no longer plays guitar the way he used to, and he says he hasn't felt genuinely happy — not *really* happy — in longer than he can remember.

He came to therapy, he says, because his daughter is twelve now, and he wants to be a father she can actually reach. He sat with that for a moment after saying it, and then looked out the window. That is the closest he has come, so far, to letting himself want something.
